topic: The Mathematical Trinity: Powers, Roots, and Logarithms

sections.title: Prerequisite: The Growth Pattern
sections.content: Briefly revisit exponentiation as repeated multiplication. Use a visual 'tree branching' animation where 2^3 represents a tree that doubles its branches 3 times, resulting in 8. This establishes the base, the exponent, and the value.
sections.example: A rabbit colony doubles (base 2) every generation (x). After 3 generations, how many rabbits? 2^3 = 8.

sections.title: Unlocking the Root: The Reverse Growth
sections.content: Introduce radicals as the inverse of powers—finding the 'seed' of the growth. Visually represent this as shrinking the tree back to its original size. Explain that the nth root is equivalent to a fractional power (1/n).
sections.example: If a square garden area is 16m², find the side length. √16 = 16^(1/2) = 4m.

sections.title: Decoding the Logarithm: Finding the Time
sections.content: Introduce the logarithm as the 'time-finder'. While powers find the total (result) and roots find the base (seed), logarithms find the exponent (time). Use a navigation analogy: 'How long until I reach the destination?'
sections.example: If the rabbit colony starts at 2 and reaches 8, how many generations passed? log₂(8) = 3.

sections.title: The Unified Notation Map
sections.content: Display a dynamic 'triangle transformation' graphic showing how a single equation (2^3=8) connects to 8^(1/3)=2 and log₂(8)=3. Emphasize that these are three ways to view the same numerical relationship.

sections.title: Summary & Quick Check
sections.content: A rapid-fire animation challenge. Show a character (a space rocket) where the exponent is the fuel burn, the root is the distance calculation, and the log is the timing required to hit the target planet.
sections.example: Mission: Reach target 100 with base 10. Exponent = 2. Log₁₀(100) = 2. Root of 100 = 10.
